 MARKET VALUE is defined as the most probable price which a property should bring in a competitive and open market under all conditions
 requisite to a fair sale, the buyer and seller each acting prudently and knowledgeably, and assuming the price is not affected by undue stimulus.
 Implicit in this definition is the consummation of a sale as of a specified date and the passing of title from seller to buyer under conditions
 whereby:
 1. buyer and seller are typically motivated;
 2. both parties are well informed or well advised and acting in what they consider their own best interests;
 3. a reasonable time is allowed for exposure in the open market;
 4. payment is made in terms of cash in U.S. dollars or in terms of financial arrangements comparable thereto; and
 5. the price represents the normal consideration for the property sold unaffected by special or creative financing or sales concessions granted by
 anyone associated with the sale. Source: The Dictionary of Real Estate Appraisal, 6th ed., Appraisal Institute

AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

WHEREAS, in Resolution 8 of 2024, the Cabot City Council authorized the City to
accept the donation of certain specified real property for use as a public park; and

WHEREAS, the Cabot City Council further authorized the City to enter into an agreement
with the Cabot Water and Waste Water Commission to provide sewer infrastructure and related
services for the proposed park. Pursuant to that agreement the Commission would also contribute

funds towards the infrastructure’s installation. The sewer infrastructure was subsequently installed and
the Commission contributed $50,705.40 to the total cost of the project; and

WHEREAS, as of the passage of this resolution, the real property in question has not been
donated to the City and, as such, has not been dedicated as a public park. The Cabot City Council
therefore determines that the infrastructure installation is not at this time in furtherance of a public
park and that the funds contributed to the project by the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission
to that end should be refunded to it.

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF CABOT,
ARKANSAS THAT:

SECTION 1: Contingent upon the conditions set forth later in this Section, the
Mayor and City Clerk~Treasurer are hereby authorized and directed to return the funds paid
by the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission pursuant to the agreement authorized by
Resolution 8 of 2024. The total amount authorized and directed to be paid to the Cabot
Water and Wastewater Commission is $50,705.40. The authorizations and directions
provided for herein shall not take effect if the real property referred to herein and in
Resolution 8 of 2024 has been acquired and by the City and dedicated as a public park by

August 30, 2025.

SECTION 2: The General Fund of the 2025 Annual Operating Budget is hereby

amended to accommodate the $50,705.40 payment authorized and directed herein.

WHEREAS, the City, in conjunction with Cabot City Beautiful, wishes to conduct
a Household Hazardous Waste Round-up event currently scheduled for March 2026;
and
WHEREAS, Ark. Code Ann § 14-58-303 et al., provides that the governing body may
waive the requirement of competitive bidding in situations where the procedure is deemed not
feasible or practical. Given the nature of the services at issue and the unknown factor of
how much and what types of hazardous waste will be disposed of, it is impossible to say
what the final cost will be and if the amount will be one that requires competitive bidding to be
used. As such, the Cabot City Council finds that competitive bidding in this matter is deemed to
be neither feasible nor practical and the requirements of competitive bidding are therefore
waived; and

WHEREAS, a service offering the removal and disposal of household hazardous waste
will be directly beneficial to the health, safety, and welfare of the people of Cabot.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF CABOT,
ARKANSAS, THAT:

SECTION 1: The Mayor and City Clerk~Treasurer are hereby authorized to enter into
an Agreement with CTS Services, Inc. to collect, bulk, containerize, transfer and recycle/dispose
of household hazardous waste during the Household Hazardous Waste Round-up event. The
agreement is authorized to be consistent with the terms in the attached Exhibit A. The City
Council recognizes that the amount of payment to CTS for these services will depend on how
much and what type of hazardous waste is disposed of at the event. Payment to CTS is
authorized to be consistent with the unit costs listed in Exhibit A.

SECTION 2: Competitive bidding for this matter is hereby deemed to be neither
feasible nor practical given the nature of the project that makes overall fixed pricing, and
therefore bidding, extremely difficult. In addition, the scope of the project, the very large variety

of types and forms of hazardous waste that could be collected, and the unknown factor of how
--- page 41 (OCR) ---
much/what manner of hazardous waste will ultimately be collected would make going through
the competitive bidding process extremely difficult, if not impossible. Moreover, there is a very
limited number of companies that offer hazardous household waste clean up services to the
extent and scope the City requires in this geographic area. As such, the Cabot City Council
hereby finds that competitive bidding for this matter would be neither feasible nor practical, and
the requirements of competitive bidding are therefore waived.

SECTION 3: This resolution shall be in full force and effect from and after its project.

Exhibit A — Scope of Services

Rodney Guthrie Drainage Study
Scope of Services

GENERAL DESCRIPTION

The Engineer will provide all professional services necessary to perform a flood hazard study of
the neighborhood along Rodney Guthrie Drive. There are several low-lying homes along
Rodney Guthrie Drive that have experienced flooding during past storm events. The watershed
drains south under the west end of Rodney Guthrie Drive, continuing south under Richie Road,
and drains southwest ultimately into Bayou Two Prairie. The approximate extent of the
proposed study area is shown in Figure 1.

Exhibit A — Scope of Services

The study is more particularly defined by Tasks 1 and 2 (Data Collection and Survey & Existing
Conditions Hydrologic and Hydraulic Modeling), and final deliverable includes a report with
recommendations for future capital improvements.

Task 1 - Data Collection and Survey

14 Data Collection and Review- Consultant shall collect and review relevant items to
be utilized for the hydrologic and hydraulic modeling effort. Data includes, but is

not limited to:
e Most recent LIDAR terrain information
e Stormwater GIS Inventory
e Stormwater Drainage Basins (provided by City)
e Existing FEMA Base Level Engineering Study

1.2 Limited Field Survey- Consultant shall determine the locations needed for field
survey based on the data review. Anticipated required field survey includes, but
is not limited to:

e Stormwater Structures (approx. 4 locations) - Measurements to verify
dimensions and invert elevations
e Open Channel cross sections (approx. 10 locations)

Task 2 - Hydrologic and Hydraulic Modeling

1) Hydrologic Modeling- Hydrologic analysis will be performed to generate flows and
hydrographs for the 1D/2D Unsteady hydraulic model. City provided drainage areas will be
subdivided to ensure adequate computational points and capture effects of significant
hydrologic features such as culverts, major outfalls, railroad crossings, and other features.
SCS Curve Number methodology will be used for infiltration and runoff parameters. NOAA
Atlas 14 will be used for precipitation estimates for design storms. The hydrologic model will
be executed for a range of storm events including the 5-, 10-, 25-, 50-, and 100-year storms.
Results of the model will be reviewed/compared to existing models, if available.

2) Hydraulic Modeling- A 1D/2D, unsteady hydraulic model will be developed to estimate water
surface elevations (WSEL) and flooding inundation for the simulated storm events.
Channels and culvert crossings will be modeled in 1D and connected to the 2D surface.
The model will reflect the most current terrain data and land use data for model parameters,
including roughness values, obstructions, and ineffective flow areas, Culverts and storm
pipes will be added to the model as needed based on GIS information and field survey data.
The hydraulic model will be executed for a range of storm events including the 5-, 10-, 25-,
50-, and 100-year storms and compared to existing models, if available.

Task 3 —- Improvement Alternatives

3) Identify improvement projects to improve drainage and reduce flooding within the basin. The
proposed improvements may consist of detention and/or conveyance improvements
including ditch widening, ditch cleanout, and culvert upsizing. Proposed improvements will
be modeled to determine flood reduction effectiveness.

Estimate buy-out costs and determine if properties would be eligible for potential hazard

5) Preliminary schematic drawings and estimates will be developed based on proposed
improvement alternatives.

ORDINANCE NO. 9 OF 2026

AN ORDINANCE ESTABLISHING ADDITIONAL INSPECTION RELATED
REQUIREMENTS FOR CITY OWNED PROPERTIES IN CERTAIN
SITUATIONS; AND OTHER PURPOSES

WHEREAS, the City of Cabot owns buildings within city limits, and multiple of said
buildings are subject to lease agreements and/or have been recently remodeled; and

WHEREAS, while the city employs building and code inspectors, the Cabot City Council
believes that city owned buildings would benefit from additional inspections performed by state
inspectors in certain circumstances; and

WHEREAS, the Cabot City Council hereby sets forth the circumstances on when
additional inspections from state inspectors are required.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of Cabot,
Arkansas that:

SECTION 1: The City must pass state level inspection(s) from any applicable state
office when a City-owned building is constructed, remodeled, or leased. Applicable City-owned
buildings that do not pass said inspection(s) may not be utilized by the City or leased to a third
party. The City must request and work in good faith to accomplish any inspection(s) required by
this Ordinance.

SECTION 2: For purposes of this Ordinance, “remodeled” refers to any construction on
or refurbishment of a City-owned building after the effective date of this Ordinance that would
require a permit under City code.

SECTION 3: For purposes of this Ordinance, “leased” buildings refer to buildings
subject to lease agreements that are executed after the effective date of this Ordinance. This
Ordinance shall not be interpreted to impose new conditions on currently enacted lease
agreements or to improperly interfere with currently enacted lease agreements.

SECTION 4: The Cabot City Council recognizes that nether it nor the City have direct
authority over state inspectors and do not have ability to mandate that state inspectors perform
the requested inspections. As such, the City shall not be in violation of this Ordinance if it
requests an inspection required herein and a representative of the applicable state office declines
the request or otherwise fails to perform the required inspection.

SECTION 5: In addition to the other requirements of this Ordinance, the City must
comply with all city ordinances, city code sections, and UDC provisions when constructing or
remodeling city-owned buildings. Additionally, the City must seek and receive Cabot Planning
Commission approval for all items required by city ordinances, city code sections, and UDC
provision when constructing or remodeling city-owned buildings.

The State of the City
March 23, 2026
To Members of the City Council and the Citizens of Cabot:
Please enjoy the slideshow behind me as I present this year's State of the City.

It is with a happy heart that I would like to report that Cabot is in a great shape. The overall state
of our city is positive and trending upward. The successful sale of property to Lyon College
school of Veterinary Medicine completed on October 31‘ 2025.

Due to the sale, in January 2026, construction began for the new Cabot Animal Support Services
(“CASS”) building, phase 1 to be completed in April 2027. The CASS building will encompass
48,000 square feet and will partner with Lyon College by holding classes out of its building until
the completion of their building, phase 2, which is projected to be completed in January of 2028.
Phase 2 will be a 2 story 48,000 square foot state of the art campus, with both buidings nestled
behind our 140,000 sports complex Game Time at the Grounds.

And with the vast success of our sports complex Game Time at The Grounds, for two months in
a row, January and February of 2026, The Grounds was ranked number one for the most visited
attractions state wide, out of 186 properties listed in this category, with 48,600 visitors in the
month of January and 57,700 visitors in February, per Placer AI.

We will also see more restaurants with the opening of Buffalo Wild Wings, McAlister’s Deli,
Cold Stone Creamery, Gion Japan House, and Old Town Coffee.

And with the recent salary increases to police and fire, our community can remain safer by
giving a competitive salary to our incoming police and firemen.

We're excited for 2026 and the great things planned for this year, but are extremely pleased with
our results from 2025.

Cabot had a very prosperous 2025. We made strides in all areas of the city. During 2025, the
following highlights occurred (this is just some of the highlights, not inclusive of all activity)
--- page 7 (OCR) ---
Community and Economic Development

Cabot experienced a year of notable achievements and steady economic growth. The city issued
187 total new business licenses and saw various commercial real estate sales.

Throughout 2025, Cabot received multiple recognitions for its dedication and hard work: In
April, the Arkansas House and Senate recognized Cabot as a Trendsetter City. In August, the city
was awarded a $499,908 Grant to expand services for residents with developmental disabilities.
And in September, Cabot earned a statewide planning award for its downtown revitalization
plan.

The local business scene welcomed several new additions, including prominent national chains
like Whataburger, a second Taco Bell, and a second Starbucks, all located on Bill Foster. We
also celebrated the opening of new local establishments such as Buckman’s Brewhouse on Main
St., Tall Paul’s, and Hangry Joes. Furthermore, Brew Ya Ya, another local favorite, relocated
and underwent a complete remodel, now situated off of Second Street in Cabot.

Police Department

The Police Department had a busy year writing 658 accident reports, 1,857 incident reports, 146
felony arrests, 340 misdemeanor arrests, 144 DWI’s, and 6599 traffic warnings resulting in 2275
traffic citations.

The Criminal Investigations Division worked 530 cases, serving 100 felony warrants, and 126
felony charges were filed. The CPD Narcotics Division had another successful year partnering
with multiple agencies across central Arkansas, bringing in 189 felony arrests, seizing $135,944
in US currency, 5.5 IBs (29,100 pills) of fentanyl, 42 IB of cocaine, and 75 IB of marijuana.

The Cabot Police Department also had a successful year promoting four officers to Sergeant, and
two officers to Lieutenant. Additionally, the police department hosted its first Cabot Police
Department Awards Banquet, recognizing and celebrating the hard work and achievements of
our officers. We handed out five Life Saving awards, four Supervisor Commendation awards,
Officer of the Year, Leadership award, Rookie of the Year, Community Service award, and Unit
Citation award.

In addition, our District Court had 6,103 new cases filed, gaining 1,551 from 2024.

The Cabot Police Department Foundation orchestrated and participated in over 20 different
community outreach and will continue to increase that number yearly.

Fire Department

In 2025, the Cabot Fire Department demonstrated continued growth, operational excellence, and
strong community commitment. One of the most significant advancements this year was the
order of a new 104-foot aerial platform apparatus, with delivery anticipated in June 2027. This
investment represents a long-term commitment to enhancing elevated rescue capabilities,
expanding firefighters reach, and ensuring readiness for future community growth.
--- page 8 (OCR) ---
Cabot Fire Department responded to over 3,500 fire and medical calls, an 8% increase from 2024
and we saved over $4 million in property value. This success is attributable to our personnel
development and training efforts being top priority. We now have five firefighters that achieved
Advanced EMT certifications, and in total 5,740 training hours thanks to the opening of the new
fire training tower- the only facility of its kind in Lonoke County. Additionally, the department
implemented a new Operations and Maintenance Officer position to enhance fleet management,
equipment oversight, and operational readiness across all divisions.

Construction Services

In 2025, Construction Services completed several impactful facility improvement projects while
continuing to provide essential daily maintenance across all city buildings. Major
accomplishments included the downstairs remodel of City Hall to integrate the Public Works and
Traffic Departments into a fully functional Municipal Building, renovations at Cabot Fire
Central Station, and repairs to Fire Station 4, Old Public Works Building, the City Annex, and
adding two new public restrooms behind City Hall to support Railyard Park and the Railyard
Pavilion.

Senior Services

The PEAK Center continued its strong upward trajectory in 2025, averaging 105 participants
each open weekday across 250 operating days, which is a significant increase from the 27-person
daily average recorded in 2021. The Center served 21,600 meals during the year, averaging 86
meals per day, compared to 24 daily meals in 2021. Transportation services remained an
essential component of accessibility, with more than 1,400 rides provided to keep participants
connected and engaged. Attendance across activities and excursions remained consistently
strong, reinforcing the PEAK Center’s role as a vibrant hub for fellowship, wellness, and active
living in Cabot.

Animal Services

Cabot Animal Support Services supported more than 9,000 families through proactive,
compassionate, and community-centered animal welfare programs that strengthen both public
safety and the human-animal bond.

CASS performed 1,588 spay/neuter surgeries, administered 8,966 vaccinations, and implanted
1,302 microchips, reducing future shelter intake and improving community health. The
department received 1,082 animals and achieved 1,101 positive outcomes, with only 16 animals
euthanized, reflecting Cabot’s continued commitment to responsible, lifesaving practices.

Street Department

We hired one new supervisor and one new laborer to help keep up with beautification and
demands of the city’s day to day operations. We purchased a new hydraulic breaking hammer for
mini-excavators. The Street Department completed 13 projects in 2025, with four future projects
in the works, those being Fairway Drive repairs, Kerr Station drainage improvements at
Barnwell Street, Kerr Station improvements from Campground Rd. to Hwy 321, and W. Locust
Street improvements from 5" St. to North 2" St. We completed 1,591 work orders, 18,686
ditches cleaned/excavated, 14,500 sq. ft. of street repairs, and 207 street light outages reported to
First Electric or Entergy for repairs.
--- page 9 (OCR) ---
Public Works

To help with the housing shortage, development of Cabot’s new housing included: Caiden Place
Subdivision (23 lots), Wolfs bridge Subdivision - Phase 2 (64 lots), Windridge Subdivision -
Phase 2 (36 lots), Going Spring Subdivision - Phase 2 (30 lots).

Major commercial growth besides Lyon College are First Arkansas Bank & Trust's new
building. Red River Ford Expansion, Cut Hill Road Expansion, Cabot High School Press Box,
and C-Store at the intersection of South 2nd and Hwy 38.

During 2025, public works had 34 accessory building permits, 7 new multi-family permits, 44
single-family remodel permits, 43 new single-family permits, 13 remodel commercial building
permits, 6 new commercial building permits. Additionally, Code Enforcement had 939 active or
worked code enforcement cases.

Financial Summary

The City of Cabot’s financial position strengthened significantly in 2025, reflecting both careful
financial management and strategic decisions that will benefit the community for years to come.

A major contributor to this improvement was the successful sale of land to Lyon College, an
investment that supports the development of higher education opportunities in Cabot while also
strengthening the City's financial foundation. In addition, revenue from the First2Connect
broadband lease continues to grow, demonstrating the long-term value of the City’s investments
in modern infrastructure and expanded connectivity. At the same time, operating expenditures
remained stable across departments, showing continued discipline in day-to-day operations. The
city also reduced its outstanding bonded debt during the year. Further improving Cabot’s long-
term financial outlook.

Conclusion

Cabot experienced a prosperous year marked by a strong financial position, significant
infrastructure improvements, and the expansion of the "Game Time at The Grounds" complex,
which ranked as the top state attraction. Key developments include the start of the 48.000 sq. ft.
Cabot Animal Support Services building, alongside major commercial growth, including new
dining establishments and residential developments to address housing needs. These results
reflect a leadership team that is investing wisely, managing responsibly, and positioning itself for
continued growth.

I cannot wait to see what the future hold for Cabot. As we enter the 50" anniversary of the
tornado that wiped out our town, we are blessed by God on where we are today.

Congratulations to all who are involved in this great year in our history as a city. May we
continue to prosper.

Respectfully,

Mayorkef Kincade

AN ORDINANCE ESTABLISHING ADDITIONAL INSPECTION RELATED
REQUIREMENTS FOR CITY OWNED PROPERTIES IN CERTAIN
SITUATIONS; AND OTHER PURPOSES

WHEREAS, the City of Cabot owns buildings within city limits, and multiple of said
buildings are subject to lease agreements and/or have been recently remodeled; and

WHEREAS, The Cabot City Council herein reaffirms its support for its own building and
code inspectors. Nothing stated herein should be read to denigrate those inspectors, however the
City Council believes that additional inspections performed by state inspectors in the
circumstances set forth herein would lead to increased transparency of the remodel and
construction process; and

WHEREAS, the Cabot City Council hereby sets forth the circumstances on when
additional inspections from state inspectors are required.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of Cabot,
Arkansas that:

SECTION 1: The City must pass state level inspection(s) from any applicable state
office when a City-owned building is constructed, remodeled, or leased. Applicable City-owned
buildings that do not pass said inspection(s) may not be utilized by the City or leased to a third
party. The City must request and work in good faith to accomplish any inspection(s) required by
this Ordinance.

SECTION 2: For purposes of this Ordinance, “constructed” refers only to the building
of a new structure in which the City or City employees act as general contractor. For purposes of
this Ordinance, “constructed” does not refer to the building of a new structure in which a third-
party company acts as general contractor.

SECTION 3: For purposes of this Ordinance, “remodeled” refers to any construction on
or refurbishment of a City-owned building after the effective date of this Ordinance that would
require a permit under City code.

SECTION 4: For purposes of this Ordinance, “leased” buildings refer to buildings
subject to lease agreements that are executed after the effective date of this Ordinance. This
Ordinance shall not be interpreted to impose new conditions on currently enacted lease
agreements or to improperly interfere with currently enacted lease agreements.

SECTION 5: The Cabot City Council recognizes that nether it nor the City have direct
authority over state inspectors and do not have ability to mandate that state inspectors perform
the requested inspections. As such, the City shall not be in violation of this Ordinance if it
requests an inspection required herein and a representative of the applicable state office declines
the request or otherwise fails to perform the required inspection.

ORDINANCE NO. 15 OF 2026
AN ORDINANCE FIXING RATES, FEES, AND DEPOSITS FOR
WATER AND OTHER WATER SERVICES RENDERED BY THE
CABOT WATER AND WASTEWATER COMMISSION; AND FOR
OTHER PURPOSES
WHEREAS, Arkansas Code Annotated § 14-234-214 provides that the water rates for
customers of a municipal waterworks system shall be fixed by the legislative body of the
municipality; and
WHEREAS, the City of Cabot, Arkansas (the “City”) has delegated responsibility for the
operations of the water and wastewater systems to the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission

(the “Commission” or “Utility”); and

WHEREAS, the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission has conducted a Rate Study in
accordance with Arkansas Act 605 of 2021 to establish Water Rates. (Exhibit A).

WHEREAS, the Commission has requested that the City approve the schedule of rates to be
charged by the Commission for Water services for customers that receive the Commission’s Water

services and those that do not receive its water services.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY
OF CABOT, ARKANSAS:

Section 1. Purpose. It is the purpose of this Ordinance to fix fair and reasonable water rates
and fees applicable to customers of the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission.
Section 2. Definitions. When used in this Ordinance, the following words and phrases shall
have the meaning as indicated:
(a) Customer Service Rate Classification;

i. Residential is a type of water or wastewater use that is directly related to
the function of a home. Residential use does not include any use associated
with the operation of any business or enterprise whether or not such
business or enterprise is operated for profit, or any in-ground lawn

irrigation system.
--- page 60 (OCR) ---
ii. Commercial is any type of water or wastewater use other than Residential,
Wholesale, Irrigation, or Hydrant water, as those terms are defined herein.

iii. Irrigation is a type of water use primarily dedicated to providing water to
plants and lawns.

iv. Non-Water Customer means a customer of the Utility receiving
wastewater services only.

v. Non-Water Customer — With Trash means a customer of the Utility
receiving wastewater services only that also receives trash-pickup services
from the City or its designee.

(b) Cut-off Date means the 25" day of the month unless the 25" day falls on a
weekend or official City holiday, in which case, Cut-off Date shall mean the first working day
following the weekend or holiday.

(c) Delinquent account means a customer account that has been disconnected or
locked-off due to non-payment of charges, fees, penalties or other assessments.

(d) Disconnected means that a properly authorized individual has adjusted the
valve assembly on a customer’s water meter such that water will not flow through the meter.

(e) Due Date means the 15" day of the month unless the 15" day falls on a
weekend or official ity holiday, in which case, Due Date shall mean the first working day following
the weekend or holiday.

(f) Hydrant is a type of water use primarily dedicated to combating fires but may

also include bulk water such as that used during construction.

(g) Lock-off means that a properly authorized individual has affixed a lock to a

Disconnected meter that shall only be removed by an authorized individual.
--- page 61 (OCR) ---
(h) Minimum Monthly Charge is the least amount that shall be billed to each
and every customer regardless of the amount of water used.

(i) Multiple-Unit Installation is a water and wastewater system that is designed
such that more than one residence or commercial unit within a structure is served water through a
single meter; such as an apartment, duplex and strip mall. A minimum monthly charge will be
accessed on each unit in a multi-unit facility.

(j) Organization Fee is a non-refundable monthly charge applied to any and all
real estate companies, agencies, landlords, and contractors who desire to have water service
temporarily connected to a property that they manage for the purpose of cleaning, repairing, or
otherwise performing maintenance of the property. The Organization Fee does not include the cost
of water usage. The Organization Fee does not apply to new construction projects.

(k) Re-connection Fee is the fee that must be paid before the reconnection of a
previously disconnected meter for any reason.

() Renter means residential water or wastewater customers who own less than a
fee interest in the property that they occupy.

(m) Special Pricing Areas are locations within the City of Cabot where customers
are required to pay increased rates to reimburse the City of Cabot for certain infrastructure costs.

(n) Voluntarily Disconnected Meter is a residential or irrigation meter that has
been Disconnected or Locked-Off by the City at the customer’s request so that the customer may
forego monthly minimum charges. Customers whose meters are voluntarily disconnected will be
required to pay a re-connection fee before water service is restored.

(0) Water Customer means a customer of the Utility receiving water service

along with wastewater services.
--- page 62 (OCR) ---
(p) Wastewater means Sanitary Sewer and related service connections to
Wastewater Collection Pipes.

Section 3. Water Service Territory. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the

Commission is authorized to extend its water-service territory to include any properties for which
a water connection exists. Any and all fees for connections shall follow Exhibit C Fees. The Utility
shall not be responsible for the costs of a new water connection.

Section 4. Disparate Rates. The City Council hereby finds and declares that Water
Customers, Non-Water Customers, and Non- Water Customers — With Trash should proportionately
share in the costs associated with the administration of the Commission and water services; thus,
the monthly water rates charged to Water Customers, Non-Water Customers, and Non-Water
Customers — With Trash should properly allocate those costs.

Section 5. Water Rates. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the monthly water
rates that are set forth in Exhibit B, “Monthly Water Rate Chart,” which is attached hereto and
incorporated herein as if set forth word for word, are fair and reasonable and reflect the minimum
rates necessary to ensure the continued operation and growth of the Utility; thus the “Monthly Water
Rate Chart” is hereby adopted and the rates reflected therein are hereby fixed as the rates to be
charged for water services to be rendered by the Utility.

(a) City-Owned Facilities. All City-owned facilities shall be billed at the
Commercial rate classification set out in Exhibit B, regardless of whether such facility would
otherwise qualify for a different rate classification.

Section 6. Fees. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the fees that are set forth
in Exhibit C, “Fee Chart,” which is attached hereto and incorporated herein as if set forth word for

word, are fair and reasonable and reflect the minimum fees necessary to ensure the continued
--- page 63 (OCR) ---
operation and growth of the Utility; thus, the “Fee Chart” is hereby adopted and the fees reflected
therein are hereby fixed as the fees to be charged for various services to be rendered by the Utility.

Section 7. Deposits. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the deposits that are
set forth in Exhibit D, “Deposit Chart’, which is attached hereto and incorporated herein as if set
forth word for word, are fair and reasonable and reflect the minimum deposits necessary to protect
the Utility from undue loss; thus, the “Deposit Chart” is hereby adopted and the deposits reflected
therein are hereby fixed as the deposits to be charged to all customers who establish water and/or
wastewater service with the Utility.

Section 8. Payment by Customers. The monthly bill is payable on the Due Date. Monthly

bills shall be based upon the volume of water and wastewater used and the applicable rate; however,
the monthly bill shall be at least the Minimum Monthly Charge, if any, as reflected on the applicable
rate.

A. Late payment and nonpayment. Any customer who does not pay his or her
bill prior to the close of the regular business day on the Due Date will be sent a late notice and
assessed both a 10% penalty and a re-billing fee. Any customer who does not pay his or her bill
prior to the close of the regular business day on the Cut-off Date will be Disconnected and may be
Locked-off. Any customer whose water service meter has been Disconnected or Locked-off by the
Utility will be assessed a Re-connection fee in addition to any and all past-due amounts, penalties,
and fees. No customer shall be reconnected unless and until all past-due amounts, penalties, and
fees, including the Re-connection fee, have been paid in full.

B. Account Termination. When an account becomes delinquent for 30 days, the
Utility shall mail notice to the location receiving service notifying the customer that the delinquent

account is being terminated. If payment is not received within 10 days, the Utility may terminate
--- page 64 (OCR) ---
the delinquent account and liquidate the customer’s deposit to offset any and all debts owed to the
Utility. The Utility may initiate collection procedures according to Arkansas law to collect any
outstanding debts remaining after application of the deposit. Any customer whose account has been
terminated due to non-payment may be required to pay an increased deposit to re-establish service.

Cc. Insufficient Checks. All returned checks or insufficient funds drafts will be
charged a check service fee as allowed by Arkansas law. If not timely paid, action will be
commenced under the Arkansas Hot Check Law and the service disconnected. All fees and
assessments as set forth in this Ordinance or any amendment thereto shall be applied. If two
returned checks or drafts are received on an account for 2 consecutive months, a letter will be mailed
to the customer stating that only certified funds or cash will be accepted for a period of one (1) year.

Dz. Billing Malfunctions. In the event of a computer hardware or software failure
or other circumstances beyond the control of the Utility, the Commission shall have full discretion
to extend the Due Date and Cut-off Date for a period of time commensurate with the delay of the
monthly billing or late notice processing.

Section 9. Billing Disputes. Billing disputes may be initiated by any customer by contacting
the Utility. Upon receipt of a billing dispute, the Utility shall perform an investigation to compile
relevant facts. Upon completing the investigation, the Utility shall compile a synopsis of the facts,
all findings of its investigation, and all documents submitted by the complainant and forward the
same to the Chairperson of the Commission for a final decision. After considering all relevant
information presented by both the Utility and the complainant, the Chairperson, or the
Chairperson’s designee, shall render a decision regarding the proper amount of the bill.

Section 10. Severability. The provisions of the Ordinance are hereby declared to be

separable and if any provision shall for any reason be held illegal or invalid, such holding shall not
--- page 65 (OCR) ---
affect the validity of the remainder of the Ordinance.
Section 11. Repealer. All parts of previous Ordinances and Resolutions in conflict
herewith are hereby repealed.

Section 12. Other Unaffected Policies. Unless in conflict with the Ordinance, all other

Ordinances, Resolutions, and Utility policies will be unchanged.

1 INTRODUCTION

The Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission DBA Cabot Waterworks has been vested with the
authority and responsibility for the proper operation, maintenance and improvement of the water and
wastewater systems of the City of Cabot pursuant to the authority provided by Arkansas Code
Annotated 88 14-234-116, and 14-234-30 I, et seq.

Cabot Waterworks, located in Cabot, Arkansas, serves a population of 27,515 through 11,127
metered connections as of 12/31/2024. This total includes master meter connections that serve
1,426 multi-unit residential customers and 154 multi-unit commercial customers, such as
apartment complexes and shopping malls. The utility is led by Tim Joyner, P.E., with Bruce Brown as
the Financial Manager. The water system currently sources water from the Alluvial aquifer, with a
maximum intake capacity of 4.0 MGD. Cabot Waterworks also has a purchase agreement with
Central Arkansas Water (CAW). This agreement includes a minimum purchase of 0.3 MGD and a
maximum of 9.0 MGD. The Arkansas Natural Resources Commission has mandated Cabot
Waterworks discontinue its groundwater well operations by 2026. Without other internal water
sources, this change would require Cabot to purchase 100% of its water from CAW. Additionally,
Cabot Waterworks maintains an emergency connection to Jacksonville Waterworks but does not
currently have a purchase agreement in place with Jacksonville.

3.1.2 Water Consumption

Water consumption significantly influences water Billed Revenue since the unit rate, charged per
1,000 gallons, applies to all customer consumption; no water usage is included in the Service Flat
Charge. Cabot Waterworks has provided 18 years of monthly recorded consumption data. By totaling
the monthly recorded consumption for each year and plotting these annual values on a chart,
projections could be developed. Similar to the population projection method, a trendline was added
to the chart. However, instead of a linear trendline, a second-order polynomial trendline proved to be
more suitable.

Two methods were used to project annual consumption, both yielding very similar results. The first
method involved comparing each month from one year to the next to determine the percentage
change in consumption. For instance, February 2015 to February 2016 showed a -0.94% change,
indicating a decrease. This process was repeated for each month across the available data, and the
percentage changes for each month over the past decade (2014-2024) were averaged. The average
percentage change for each month was then applied to the most recent monthly recorded data,
projecting consumption for each month over the study period. The monthly totals were summed to
provide annual consumption projections.

The second approach involved comparing year-to-year consumption changes and calculating the
average percent growth over the past decade. This average growth rate was then applied to the most
recent recorded year's total consumption. Both projection methods produced comparable results,
as illustrated in Figure 3-3.

4 FORECASTING FINANCIAL RESULTS

This section presents financial projections for Cabot Waterworks, considering both a transition to a
100% purchased water agreement with CAW and maintaining the current purchase agreement. Most
O&M and G&A expenses will be projected with a 4% annual increase applied to 2024’s recorded

4.1 Purchased Water

Cabot Waterworks currently relies on groundwater as its primary water source. However, as
discussed earlier in this report, it will be required to discontinue using groundwater by 2026. This
transition could require Cabot Waterworks to purchase all of its water supply from Central Arkansas
Water (CAW), which will significantly increase purchase water expenses due to both the higher
volume of purchased water and the scheduled rate increases set by CAW (CAW’s Rate schedule is
provided in the Appendix of this report).

Currently, Cabot Waterworks purchases 0.3 MGD from CAW, which is approximately 11.87% of its
total water use projected for 2025. To assess the financial implications of maintaining this purchase
agreement versus transitioning to 100% purchased water, two projections have been made:

e Table 4-1 presents the projected purchase water expenses if Cabot Waterworks transitions
to fully purchasing its water from CAW.

MGD.

Under the current agreement with CAW, the percentage of water purchased is used to determine
additional charges on top of the Master Meter Fee and unit rate. These charges include the
Development Fee, Watershed Protection Fee, and Infrastructure Fee. For example, Cabot
Waterworks pays only the percentage of the Infrastructure Fee per meter that corresponds to the
percentage of water purchased from CAW. However, if the system transitions to 100% purchased
water, these fees will increase proportionally.

water loss. Using the projected annual consumption increase of 1.35%, the same growth rate will be

4.4 Forecasting Revenue v. Expenses

The model methodology outlined in Section 3, for billed revenue projections will be used to compare
forecasted revenue and expenses. Non-rate revenue will be projected with a 3% annual increase, and
this impact is reflected in the updated revenue projections.

e Table 4-4 presents the projected revenue and expenses if Cabot Waterworks transitions to
100% purchased water from CAW.

e Table 4-5 displays the projected revenue and expenses if Cabot Waterworks remains with the
current purchase agreement, continuing to purchase only 0.3 MGD of its total water use from
CAW. Unlike the 100% purchase scenario, O&M expenses will not decrease in this case, as
the costs associated with maintaining the existing groundwater infrastructure will persist.

The financial impact of transitioning to 100% purchased water from CAW versus maintaining the
current purchase agreement presents key differences:

e Transitioning to 100% purchased water significantly increases total expenses due to higher
purchased water volume, scheduled CAW rate increases, and additional fees such as the
Infrastructure Fee, Watershed Protection Fee, and Development Fee. As a result, a larger net
deficit is projected, particularly in 2026 when the full transition takes effect.

e Maintaining the current purchase agreement avoids the higher costs associated with 100%
purchased water by maintaining the existing groundwater system. While this scenario
reduces dependency on CAW’s rate structure, continued investment in infrastructure and
potential capital improvements may still be necessary.

While moving to fully purchased water simplifies operations, it comes at a higher financial cost.
Without rate adjustments, Cabot Waterworks will face growing deficits under both scenarios. Rising
costs for materials, fuel, and maintenance further strain financial stability. To account for inflation
and operational cost growth, a 4% annual increase has been applied to 2024’s recorded O&M
expenses outside of purchased water and public safety, as well as all general and administrative
(G&A) expenses. Public safety expenses will remain at 5% of water billed revenue plus $35,000 in
Lieu of City Taxes, while a 5% gross revenue allocation for repairs and refurbishments will also be
applied.

To maintain financial sustainability, a rate increase will be necessary to cover the rising cost of
purchased water. However, operating expenses, regulatory compliance, and_ infrastructure
investments are adequately funded under the current rate structure, provided there are no changes
to the purchase agreement with CAW.

5 WATER RATE INCREASE

Rising costs across multiple areas—including purchased water expenses, operations, maintenance,
and infrastructure—necessitate a rate adjustment to maintain financial stability. This section
presents two rate results scenarios to address these increasing expenses:

e Section 5.1 outlines the unit rate increase per customer for 100% purchased water
agreement.

e Section 5.2 outlines a rate increase if Cabot Waterworks transitions to purchasing 100% of
its water from CAW.

e Section 5.3 details the rate results if the utility maintains its current purchase agreement with
CAW, continuing to produce most of its water while purchasing a smaller portion.

e Section 5.4 provides a comparative analysis of the resulting average customer bills.

Through the water model projection process, various rate structures can be evaluated to assess their
financial impact. When considering rate adjustments, factors such as the effect on different
customer groups and the need to cover rising expenses—particularly in purchased water, operations,
and maintenance—must be addressed.

One approach is adjusting the unit rate, ensuring revenue aligns with increasing costs tied to water
consumption. Alternatively, incorporating these expenses into the Service Flat Charge, similar to the
debt service fee, may not fully account for the variable nature of purchased water and operational
costs. Another option is implementing targeted fees to address specific cost drivers.

Ultimately, the selected rate adjustments must enable Cabot Waterworks to meet its financial
obligations while maintaining reliable service and infrastructure.

5.1 Unit Rate Increase CAW

Table 5-1 presents the annual unit rate (cost per 1,000 gallons) from CAW, which is added to all
existing unit rate thresholds. This rate increases each year as purchased water costs rise.

To determine the unit cost, the shortfall revenue due to purchased water (Identified in Table 4-4) is
divided by the projected billed water volume and converted to a per-1,000-gallon basis. This ensures
that the necessary rate adjustments are applied to each customer class and unit rate threshold.

As you know, I was asked to look into options for the City to procure a gun range for use as a police
training facility.

roof. As we explored this option, we determined that it lacked the ease of implementation, flexibility of
function, and ability to expand for additional gun range purposes that the City and the Police Department
needed in this project. This option did not fit our needs. Reducing the range in size would affect the
Department’s need for a tactical range for training, thus reducing the training function. Going this route
would’ve been a poor use of public funds and not delivered on what the Police department ultimately
required.

vendors, to find additional options. I found one company with a product that would meet the Police

explored and is exactly what the City needs. This system is the intellectual property of D5 Ranges and
DS Ranges is the sole source for that system.

They can install the Range with Plumbing, Electrical, HVAC and concrete slab for $2,500,000.00.

1 INTRODUCTION
The Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission DBA Cabot Waterworks has been vested with the
authority and responsibility for the proper operation, maintenance and improvement of the water and
wastewater systems of the City of Cabot pursuant to the authority provided by Arkansas Code
Annotated §§ 14-234-116, and 14-234-30 I, et seq.

Cabot Waterworks, located in Cabot, Arkansas, serves a population of 27,515 through 11,127
metered connections as of 12/31/2024. This total includes master meter connections that serve
1,426 multi-unit residential customers and 154 multi-unit commercial customers, such as
apartment complexes and shopping malls. The utility is led by Tim Joyner, P.E., with Bruce Brown as
the Financial Manager. The water system currently sources water from the Alluvial aquifer, with a
maximum intake capacity of 4.0 MGD. Cabot Waterworks also has a purchase agreement with
Central Arkansas Water (CAW). This agreement includes a minimum purchase of 0.3 MGD and a
maximum of 9.0 MGD. The Arkansas Natural Resources Commission has mandated Cabot
Waterworks discontinue its groundwater well operations by 2026. Without other internal water
sources, this change would require Cabot to purchase 100% of its water from CAW. Additionally,
Cabot Waterworks maintains an emergency connection to Jacksonville Waterworks but does not
currently have a purchase agreement in place with Jacksonville.

Unit Rate 2 applies, also charged per 1,000 gallons.

2.5 Tracking Water Financial Records for Forecasting
This section reviews recorded revenue and expenses since 2022 to forecast future financial trends.
This rate study uses a forecast based on historical growth trends.

2.5.1 Revenue
Revenue sources include both billed and non-rate income. Billed revenue comes from residential
(metered inside, and outside city limits, and multi-unit), commercial (metered and multi-unit), and
sprinkler connections. Non-rate revenue includes fees from new connections, disconnections, late
charges, returned checks, interest, antenna leases, sales tax discounts, and other miscellaneous
sources.

2.5.2 Expenses
Cabot Waterworks categorizes expenses into Operations & Maintenance (O&M) and General &
Administrative (G&A). Purchased water and public safety, while part of O&M, are highlighted
separately but included in the total O&M calculation.

G&A expenses have also been separated to distinguish water-specific G&A costs from shared office
G&A expenses, which are currently funded through an 80/20 split between water and wastewater
revenue, with water covering 80% of the shared costs.

2.6 Analysis Summary
Cabot Waterworks has seen growth in both revenue and expenses over the study period. However,

 • Expenses will be projected with a 4% annual increase, based on recorded expenses.
 • Non-rate revenue will be projected with a 3% annual increase, aligned with the historical
 growth.

revenue, providing the foundation for financial forecasting. Section 4 will then compare the projected
revenue with forecasted expenses to ensure financial feasibility and sustainability.

displays the recorded population from 1970, with a linear trendline to support projections. Using the

3.1.2 Water Consumption
Water consumption significantly influences water Billed Revenue since the unit rate, charged per
1,000 gallons, applies to all customer consumption; no water usage is included in the Service Flat
Charge. Cabot Waterworks has provided 18 years of monthly recorded consumption data. By totaling
the monthly recorded consumption for each year and plotting these annual values on a chart,
projections could be developed. Similar to the population projection method, a trendline was added
to the chart. However, instead of a linear trendline, a second-order polynomial trendline proved to be
more suitable.

Two methods were used to project annual consumption, both yielding very similar results. The first
method involved comparing each month from one year to the next to determine the percentage
change in consumption. For instance, February 2015 to February 2016 showed a -0.94% change,
indicating a decrease. This process was repeated for each month across the available data, and the
percentage changes for each month over the past decade (2014–2024) were averaged. The average
percentage change for each month was then applied to the most recent monthly recorded data,
projecting consumption for each month over the study period. The monthly totals were summed to
provide annual consumption projections.

The second approach involved comparing year-to-year consumption changes and calculating the
average percent growth over the past decade. This average growth rate was then applied to the most
recent recorded year's total consumption. Both projection methods produced comparable results,
as illustrated in Figure 3-3.

3.2.3 Projecting Annual Unit Rate 2 Revenue
To project the annual revenue from Unit Rate 2, first calculate the consumption under the Unit Rate

customers exceeding 5,000 gallons per month, multiply the total connections (TC) by the percentage
of connections over 5,000 gallons (%>5K) and then by 5,000 gallons. Add these two products and
multiply by 12 to annualize this amount, giving the estimated annual consumption under Unit Rate
1.

to find the remaining consumption applicable to Unit Rate 2. Convert this remaining consumption to
thousands of gallons, then multiply by Unit Rate 2 (UR2) to estimate the annual revenue from Unit

4 FORECASTING FINANCIAL RESULTS
This section presents financial projections for Cabot Waterworks, considering both a transition to a
100% purchased water agreement with CAW and maintaining the current purchase agreement. Most
O&M and G&A expenses will be projected with a 4% annual increase applied to 2024’s recorded
expenses, as identified in Section 2.6. Additionally, a 3% annual increase will be applied to all non-
rate revenue, while billed revenue will be projected using the model methodology outlined in Section
3.

4.1 Purchased Water
Cabot Waterworks currently relies on groundwater as its primary water source. However, as
discussed earlier in this report, it will be required to discontinue using groundwater by 2026. This
transition could require Cabot Waterworks to purchase all of its water supply from Central Arkansas
Water (CAW), which will significantly increase purchase water expenses due to both the higher
volume of purchased water and the scheduled rate increases set by CAW (CAW’s Rate schedule is
provided in the Appendix of this report).

Currently, Cabot Waterworks purchases 0.3 MGD from CAW, which is approximately 11.87% of its
total water use projected for 2025. To assess the financial implications of maintaining this purchase

The model methodology outlined in Section 3, for billed revenue projections will be used to compare
forecasted revenue and expenses. Non-rate revenue will be projected with a 3% annual increase, and

 current purchase agreement, continuing to purchase only 0.3 MGD of its total water use from

The financial impact of transitioning to 100% purchased water from CAW versus maintaining the
current purchase agreement presents key differences:

 • Transitioning to 100% purchased water significantly increases total expenses due to higher
 purchased water volume, scheduled CAW rate increases, and additional fees such as the
 Infrastructure Fee, Watershed Protection Fee, and Development Fee. As a result, a larger net
 deficit is projected, particularly in 2026 when the full transition takes effect.
 • Maintaining the current purchase agreement avoids the higher costs associated with 100%
 purchased water by maintaining the existing groundwater system. While this scenario
 reduces dependency on CAW’s rate structure, continued investment in infrastructure and
 potential capital improvements may still be necessary.

While moving to fully purchased water simplifies operations, it comes at a higher financial cost.
Without rate adjustments, Cabot Waterworks will face growing deficits under both scenarios. Rising
costs for materials, fuel, and maintenance further strain financial stability. To account for inflation
and operational cost growth, a 4% annual increase has been applied to 2024’s recorded O&M
expenses outside of purchased water and public safety, as well as all general and administrative
(G&A) expenses. Public safety expenses will remain at 5% of water billed revenue plus $35,000 in
Lieu of City Taxes, while a 5% gross revenue allocation for repairs and refurbishments will also be
applied.

To maintain financial sustainability, a rate increase will be necessary to cover the rising cost of
purchased water. However, operating expenses, regulatory compliance, and infrastructure
investments are adequately funded under the current rate structure, provided there are no changes
to the purchase agreement with CAW.

5 WATER RATE INCREASE
Rising costs across multiple areas—including purchased water expenses, operations, maintenance,
and infrastructure—necessitate a rate adjustment to maintain financial stability. This section
presents two rate results scenarios to address these increasing expenses:

 • Section 5.1 outlines the unit rate increase per customer for 100% purchased water
 agreement.
 • Section 5.2 outlines a rate increase if Cabot Waterworks transitions to purchasing 100% of
 its water from CAW.
 • Section 5.3 details the rate results if the utility maintains its current purchase agreement with
 CAW, continuing to produce most of its water while purchasing a smaller portion.
 • Section 5.4 provides a comparative analysis of the resulting average customer bills.

Through the water model projection process, various rate structures can be evaluated to assess their
financial impact. When considering rate adjustments, factors such as the effect on different
customer groups and the need to cover rising expenses—particularly in purchased water, operations,
and maintenance—must be addressed.

One approach is adjusting the unit rate, ensuring revenue aligns with increasing costs tied to water
consumption. Alternatively, incorporating these expenses into the Service Flat Charge, similar to the
debt service fee, may not fully account for the variable nature of purchased water and operational
costs. Another option is implementing targeted fees to address specific cost drivers.

Ultimately, the selected rate adjustments must enable Cabot Waterworks to meet its financial
obligations while maintaining reliable service and infrastructure.

AN ORDINANCE ESTABLISHING ADDITIONAL INSPECTION RELATED
REQUIREMENTS FOR CITY OWNED PROPERTIES IN CERTAIN
SITUATIONS; AND OTHER PURPOSES

WHEREAS, the City of Cabot owns buildings within city limits, and multiple of said
buildings are subject to lease agreements and/or have been recently remodeled; and

WHEREAS, The Cabot City Council herein reaffirms its support for its own building and
code inspectors. Nothing stated herein should be read to denigrate those inspectors, however the
City Council believes that additional inspections performed by state inspectors in the
circumstances set forth herein would lead to increased transparency of the remodel and
construction process; and

WHEREAS, the Cabot City Council hereby sets forth the circumstances on when
additional inspections from state inspectors are required.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of Cabot,
Arkansas that:

SECTION 1: The City must pass state level inspection(s) from any applicable state
office when a City-owned building is constructed, remodeled, or leased. Applicable City-owned
buildings that do not pass said inspection(s) may not be utilized by the City or leased to a third
party. The City must request and work in good faith to accomplish any inspection(s) required by
this Ordinance.

SECTION 2: For purposes of this Ordinance, “constructed” refers only to the building
of a new structure in which the City or City employees act as general contractor. For purposes of
this Ordinance, “constructed” does not refer to the building of a new structure in which a third-
party company acts as general contractor.

SECTION 3: For purposes of this Ordinance, “remodeled” refers to any construction on
or refurbishment of a City-owned building after the effective date of this Ordinance that would
require a permit under City code.

SECTION 4: For purposes of this Ordinance, “leased” buildings refer to buildings
subject to lease agreements that are executed after the effective date of this Ordinance. This
Ordinance shall not be interpreted to impose new conditions on currently enacted lease
agreements or to improperly interfere with currently enacted lease agreements.

SECTION 5: The Cabot City Council recognizes that nether it nor the City have direct
authority over state inspectors and do not have ability to mandate that state inspectors perform
the requested inspections. As such, the City shall not be in violation of this Ordinance if it
requests an inspection required herein and a representative of the applicable state office declines
the request or otherwise fails to perform the required inspection.

Sanitation Revenue and Margin Analysis — 2025

The sanitation rate structure included an estimated margin of approximately $0.45 per billed
account. Based on 108,475 accounts billed during 2025, this equates to an expected margin
of $48,813.75.

However, the City does not retain this full amount due to three primary factors: revenue
reductions prior to receipt, billing costs, and timing differences associated with accounting.

41 Expected Margin $48,813.75 $0.45
2 Less: Bad Debt & Allocation Adjustments ($10,997.42) ($0.10)
3 Less: Billing Expense ($21,971.96) ($0.20)
4 Remaining (Before Timing Differences) $15,844.37 $0.15
5 Less: Timing Differences ($6,032.78) ($0.06)
6 Final Net Retained by City $9,811.59 $0.09

Bad debt and allocation adjustments represent amounts billed to customers but not collected
by WaterWorks, These reductions occur prior to revenue being remitted to the City and
therefore reduce the effective margin.

Billing expense represents the annual cost paid to WaterWorks to administer sanitation billing.

We record the expense when the service happens, but we don’t record the revenue until after
WaterWorks bills and collects and then sends it to us. So the expense shows up first and the
revenue shows up later. That creates a timing gap in the year, even though the money is
coming in.

After accounting for all factors, the City’s actual retained amount for 2025 was $9,811.59,
which equates to approximately $0.09 per billed account.

This demonstrates that the nominal $0.45 margin is significantly reduced in practice due to
operational and structural factors.

ORDINANCE NO. 15 OF 2026
AN ORDINANCE FIXING RATES, FEES, AND DEPOSITS FOR
WATER AND OTHER WATER SERVICES RENDERED BY THE
CABOT WATER AND WASTEWATER COMMISSION; AND FOR
OTHER PURPOSES
WHEREAS, Arkansas Code Annotated § 14-234-214 provides that the water rates for
customers of a municipal waterworks system shall be fixed by the legislative body of the
municipality; and
WHEREAS, the City of Cabot, Arkansas (the “City”) has delegated responsibility for the
operations of the water and wastewater systems to the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission

(the “Commission” or “Utility”); and

WHEREAS, the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission has conducted a Rate Study in
accordance with Arkansas Act 605 of 2021 to establish Water Rates. (Exhibit A).

WHEREAS, the Commission has requested that the City approve the schedule of rates to be
charged by the Commission for Water services for customers that receive the Commission’s Water

services and those that do not receive its water services.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY
OF CABOT, ARKANSAS:

Section 1. Purpose. It is the purpose of this Ordinance to fix fair and reasonable water rates
and fees applicable to customers of the Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission.
Section 2. Definitions. When used in this Ordinance, the following words and phrases shall
have the meaning as indicated:
(a) Customer Service Rate Classification;

i. Residential is a type of water or wastewater use that is directly related to
the function of a home. Residential use does not include any use associated
with the operation of any business or enterprise whether or not such
business or enterprise is operated for profit, or any in-ground lawn

irrigation system.
--- page 68 (OCR) ---
ii. Commercial is any type of water or wastewater use other than Residential,
Wholesale, Irrigation, or Hydrant water, as those terms are defined herein.

iii. Irrigation is a type of water use primarily dedicated to providing water to
plants and lawns.

iv. Non-Water Customer means a customer of the Utility receiving
wastewater services only.

v. Non-Water Customer — With Trash means a customer of the Utility
receiving wastewater services only that also receives trash-pickup services
from the City or its designee.

(b) Cut-off Date means the 25" day of the month unless the 25" day falls on a
weekend or official City holiday, in which case, Cut-off Date shall mean the first working day
following the weekend or holiday.

(c) Delinquent account means a customer account that has been disconnected or
locked-off due to non-payment of charges, fees, penalties or other assessments.

(d) Disconnected means that a properly authorized individual has adjusted the
valve assembly on a customer’s water meter such that water will not flow through the meter.

(e) Due Date means the 15" day of the month unless the 15" day falls on a
weekend or official ity holiday, in which case, Due Date shall mean the first working day following
the weekend or holiday.

(f) Hydrant is a type of water use primarily dedicated to combating fires but may

also include bulk water such as that used during construction.

(g) Lock-off means that a properly authorized individual has affixed a lock to a

Disconnected meter that shall only be removed by an authorized individual.
--- page 69 (OCR) ---
(h) Minimum Monthly Charge is the least amount that shall be billed to each
and every customer regardless of the amount of water used.

(i) Multiple-Unit Installation is a water and wastewater system that is designed
such that more than one residence or commercial unit within a structure is served water through a
single meter; such as an apartment, duplex and strip mall. A minimum monthly charge will be
accessed on each unit in a multi-unit facility.

(j) Organization Fee is a non-refundable monthly charge applied to any and all
real estate companies, agencies, landlords, and contractors who desire to have water service
temporarily connected to a property that they manage for the purpose of cleaning, repairing, or
otherwise performing maintenance of the property. The Organization Fee does not include the cost
of water usage. The Organization Fee does not apply to new construction projects.

(k) Re-connection Fee is the fee that must be paid before the reconnection of a
previously disconnected meter for any reason.

() Renter means residential water or wastewater customers who own less than a
fee interest in the property that they occupy.

(m) Special Pricing Areas are locations within the City of Cabot where customers
are required to pay increased rates to reimburse the City of Cabot for certain infrastructure costs.

(n) Voluntarily Disconnected Meter is a residential or irrigation meter that has
been Disconnected or Locked-Off by the City at the customer’s request so that the customer may
forego monthly minimum charges. Customers whose meters are voluntarily disconnected will be
required to pay a re-connection fee before water service is restored.

(0) Water Customer means a customer of the Utility receiving water service

along with wastewater services.
--- page 70 (OCR) ---
(p) Wastewater means Sanitary Sewer and related service connections to
Wastewater Collection Pipes.

Section 3. Water Service Territory. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the

Commission is authorized to extend its water-service territory to include any properties for which
a water connection exists. Any and all fees for connections shall follow Exhibit C Fees. The Utility
shall not be responsible for the costs of a new water connection.

Section 4. Disparate Rates. The City Council hereby finds and declares that Water
Customers, Non-Water Customers, and Non- Water Customers — With Trash should proportionately
share in the costs associated with the administration of the Commission and water services; thus,
the monthly water rates charged to Water Customers, Non-Water Customers, and Non-Water
Customers — With Trash should properly allocate those costs.

Section 5. Water Rates. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the monthly water
rates that are set forth in Exhibit B, “Monthly Water Rate Chart,” which is attached hereto and
incorporated herein as if set forth word for word, are fair and reasonable and reflect the minimum
rates necessary to ensure the continued operation and growth of the Utility; thus the “Monthly Water
Rate Chart” is hereby adopted and the rates reflected therein are hereby fixed as the rates to be
charged for water services to be rendered by the Utility.

(a) City-Owned Facilities. All City-owned facilities shall be billed at the
Commercial rate classification set out in Exhibit B, regardless of whether such facility would
otherwise qualify for a different rate classification.

Section 6. Fees. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the fees that are set forth
in Exhibit C, “Fee Chart,” which is attached hereto and incorporated herein as if set forth word for

word, are fair and reasonable and reflect the minimum fees necessary to ensure the continued
--- page 71 (OCR) ---
operation and growth of the Utility; thus, the “Fee Chart” is hereby adopted and the fees reflected
therein are hereby fixed as the fees to be charged for various services to be rendered by the Utility.

Section 7. Deposits. The City Council hereby finds and declares that the deposits that are
set forth in Exhibit D, “Deposit Chart’, which is attached hereto and incorporated herein as if set
forth word for word, are fair and reasonable and reflect the minimum deposits necessary to protect
the Utility from undue loss; thus, the “Deposit Chart” is hereby adopted and the deposits reflected
therein are hereby fixed as the deposits to be charged to all customers who establish water and/or
wastewater service with the Utility.

Section 8. Payment by Customers. The monthly bill is payable on the Due Date. Monthly

bills shall be based upon the volume of water and wastewater used and the applicable rate; however,
the monthly bill shall be at least the Minimum Monthly Charge, if any, as reflected on the applicable
rate.

A. Late payment and nonpayment. Any customer who does not pay his or her
bill prior to the close of the regular business day on the Due Date will be sent a late notice and
assessed both a 10% penalty and a re-billing fee. Any customer who does not pay his or her bill
prior to the close of the regular business day on the Cut-off Date will be Disconnected and may be
Locked-off. Any customer whose water service meter has been Disconnected or Locked-off by the
Utility will be assessed a Re-connection fee in addition to any and all past-due amounts, penalties,
and fees. No customer shall be reconnected unless and until all past-due amounts, penalties, and
fees, including the Re-connection fee, have been paid in full.

B. Account Termination. When an account becomes delinquent for 30 days, the
Utility shall mail notice to the location receiving service notifying the customer that the delinquent

account is being terminated. If payment is not received within 10 days, the Utility may terminate
--- page 72 (OCR) ---
the delinquent account and liquidate the customer’s deposit to offset any and all debts owed to the
Utility. The Utility may initiate collection procedures according to Arkansas law to collect any
outstanding debts remaining after application of the deposit. Any customer whose account has been
terminated due to non-payment may be required to pay an increased deposit to re-establish service.

Cc. Insufficient Checks. All returned checks or insufficient funds drafts will be
charged a check service fee as allowed by Arkansas law. If not timely paid, action will be
commenced under the Arkansas Hot Check Law and the service disconnected. All fees and
assessments as set forth in this Ordinance or any amendment thereto shall be applied. If two
returned checks or drafts are received on an account for 2 consecutive months, a letter will be mailed
to the customer stating that only certified funds or cash will be accepted for a period of one (1) year.

Dz. Billing Malfunctions. In the event of a computer hardware or software failure
or other circumstances beyond the control of the Utility, the Commission shall have full discretion
to extend the Due Date and Cut-off Date for a period of time commensurate with the delay of the
monthly billing or late notice processing.

Section 9. Billing Disputes. Billing disputes may be initiated by any customer by contacting
the Utility. Upon receipt of a billing dispute, the Utility shall perform an investigation to compile
relevant facts. Upon completing the investigation, the Utility shall compile a synopsis of the facts,
all findings of its investigation, and all documents submitted by the complainant and forward the
same to the Chairperson of the Commission for a final decision. After considering all relevant
information presented by both the Utility and the complainant, the Chairperson, or the
Chairperson’s designee, shall render a decision regarding the proper amount of the bill.

Section 10. Severability. The provisions of the Ordinance are hereby declared to be

separable and if any provision shall for any reason be held illegal or invalid, such holding shall not
--- page 73 (OCR) ---
affect the validity of the remainder of the Ordinance.
Section 11. Repealer. All parts of previous Ordinances and Resolutions in conflict
herewith are hereby repealed.

Section 12. Other Unaffected Policies. Unless in conflict with the Ordinance, all other

Ordinances, Resolutions, and Utility policies will be unchanged.

1 INTRODUCTION

The Cabot Water and Wastewater Commission DBA Cabot Waterworks has been vested with the
authority and responsibility for the proper operation, maintenance and improvement of the water and
wastewater systems of the City of Cabot pursuant to the authority provided by Arkansas Code
Annotated 88 14-234-116, and 14-234-30 I, et seq.

Cabot Waterworks, located in Cabot, Arkansas, serves a population of 27,515 through 11,127
metered connections as of 12/31/2024. This total includes master meter connections that serve
1,426 multi-unit residential customers and 154 multi-unit commercial customers, such as
apartment complexes and shopping malls. The utility is led by Tim Joyner, P.E., with Bruce Brown as
the Financial Manager. The water system currently sources water from the Alluvial aquifer, with a
maximum intake capacity of 4.0 MGD. Cabot Waterworks also has a purchase agreement with
Central Arkansas Water (CAW). This agreement includes a minimum purchase of 0.3 MGD and a
maximum of 9.0 MGD. The Arkansas Natural Resources Commission has mandated Cabot
Waterworks discontinue its groundwater well operations by 2026. Without other internal water
sources, this change would require Cabot to purchase 100% of its water from CAW. Additionally,
Cabot Waterworks maintains an emergency connection to Jacksonville Waterworks but does not
currently have a purchase agreement in place with Jacksonville.

3.1.2 Water Consumption

Water consumption significantly influences water Billed Revenue since the unit rate, charged per
1,000 gallons, applies to all customer consumption; no water usage is included in the Service Flat
Charge. Cabot Waterworks has provided 18 years of monthly recorded consumption data. By totaling
the monthly recorded consumption for each year and plotting these annual values on a chart,
projections could be developed. Similar to the population projection method, a trendline was added
to the chart. However, instead of a linear trendline, a second-order polynomial trendline proved to be
more suitable.

Two methods were used to project annual consumption, both yielding very similar results. The first
method involved comparing each month from one year to the next to determine the percentage
change in consumption. For instance, February 2015 to February 2016 showed a -0.94% change,
indicating a decrease. This process was repeated for each month across the available data, and the
percentage changes for each month over the past decade (2014-2024) were averaged. The average
percentage change for each month was then applied to the most recent monthly recorded data,
projecting consumption for each month over the study period. The monthly totals were summed to
provide annual consumption projections.

The second approach involved comparing year-to-year consumption changes and calculating the
average percent growth over the past decade. This average growth rate was then applied to the most
recent recorded year's total consumption. Both projection methods produced comparable results,
as illustrated in Figure 3-3.

4 FORECASTING FINANCIAL RESULTS

This section presents financial projections for Cabot Waterworks, considering both a transition to a
100% purchased water agreement with CAW and maintaining the current purchase agreement. Most
O&M and G&A expenses will be projected with a 4% annual increase applied to 2024’s recorded
expenses, as identified in Section 2.6. Additionally, a 3% annual increase will be applied to all non-
rate revenue, while billed revenue will be projected using the model methodology outlined in Section

4.1 Purchased Water

Cabot Waterworks currently relies on groundwater as its primary water source. However, as
discussed earlier in this report, it will be required to discontinue using groundwater by 2026. This
transition could require Cabot Waterworks to purchase all of its water supply from Central Arkansas
Water (CAW), which will significantly increase purchase water expenses due to both the higher
volume of purchased water and the scheduled rate increases set by CAW (CAW’s Rate schedule is
provided in the Appendix of this report).

Currently, Cabot Waterworks purchases 0.3 MGD from CAW, which is approximately 11.87% of its
total water use projected for 2025. To assess the financial implications of maintaining this purchase
agreement versus transitioning to 100% purchased water, two projections have been made:

e Table 4-1 presents the projected purchase water expenses if Cabot Waterworks transitions
to fully purchasing its water from CAW.

MGD.

Under the current agreement with CAW, the percentage of water purchased is used to determine
additional charges on top of the Master Meter Fee and unit rate. These charges include the
Development Fee, Watershed Protection Fee, and Infrastructure Fee. For example, Cabot
Waterworks pays only the percentage of the Infrastructure Fee per meter that corresponds to the
percentage of water purchased from CAW. However, if the system transitions to 100% purchased
water, these fees will increase proportionally.

water loss. Using the projected annual consumption increase of 1.35%, the same growth rate will be
